extracted.intended_audience: law students, practitioners, scholars, and general readers interested in U.S. administrative law and Supreme Court decisions
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the legal standards from Citizens to Preserve Overton Park v. Volpe governing when agencies may approve use of federal funds for construction through public parks and the scope/standard of judicial review under the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: No feasible and prudent alternative requirement (DOT Act §4(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of Transportation can only approve use of federal funds for construction of a highway in a public park if no feasible and prudent alternative exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a statutory precondition under §4(f) of the Department of Transportation Act: financing interstate construction through public parks is prohibited if a 'feasible and prudent' alternative route exists. The Court characterized §4(f) as a 'plain and explicit bar' to such uses of federal funds, giving parkland protection paramount importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to undertake all possible planning to minimize harm (DOT Act §4(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: If no feasible and prudent alternative exists, the Secretary may allow construction only after undertaking all possible planning to minimize harm to the park.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory clause requires affirmative planning steps to minimize harm before approval. The Court found that mere reliance on litigation affidavits was insufficient evidence that such planning had been undertaken in the present case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'prudent' cannot be mere cost–benefit weighing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court rejected the Secretary's interpretation of 'prudent' as permitting a balancing of costs and benefits to determine whether alternatives exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because pre-1966 construction showed relatively low costs of avoiding parks, Congress intended to give park protection paramount importance; agencies may not short-circuit this by treating 'prudent' as an open-ended cost–benefit discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA §701(a)(2) 'committed to agency discretion' exception is very narrow ('no law to apply' doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Procedure Act's Section 701(a)(2) exception from judicial review applies only when statutes are 'drawn in such broad terms that in a given case there is no law to apply.' The Court described the exception as 'very narrow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'no law to apply' doctrine is rarely met because Congress typically provides statutory guidance; thus most agency actions remain reviewable and are not shielded by §701(a)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review: 'arbitrary or capricious' under APA §706 (the 'hard look' doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the agency's decision was informal adjudication, it is reviewable under the 'arbitrary or capricious' standard of Section 706 of the APA; courts must examine the entire record and take a 'hard look' at agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overton Park marked the requirement that courts scrutinize the administrative record thoroughly; later cases (e.g., State Farm) expanded on this 'hard look' review. In practice, courts will evaluate whether the agency articulated a rational connection between facts and its decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative record and evidence sufficiency for review
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency's sole reliance on litigation affidavits was insufficient to support summary judgment and to permit meaningful judicial review; while formal findings are not required, the record must be adequate for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require an administrative record that allows review under §706; affidavits filed during litigation generally do not substitute for an agency's contemporaneous administrative record and reasoning. Insufficient record evidence can require reversal and remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial option on review: vacate/ remand for further proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where judicial review reveals inadequacy in the agency's decision or record, courts may vacate summary judgment and remand the matter for further proceedings (either to the district court for factfinding or back to the agency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Overton Park the Supreme Court vacated the grant of summary judgment and remanded for further proceedings; the majority remanded to the District Court while a dissent would have remanded directly to the Secretary, illustrating possible remedial paths.
